prompt: Why does a layout on a phone not give sizes in physical pixels?

choices.text: Pixels are too small a unit for whole screens
choices.why: The size of the number is not the problem; what one pixel measures is.

choices.text: Only iOS allows pixels in layouts
choices.why: Neither platform lays out in pixels; both use a density-independent unit.

choices.text: A pixel's physical size differs from screen to screen
choices.why: Right. The same pixel count is a big button on one phone and a small one on another.

choices.text: Pixels cannot hold fractions
choices.why: Fractions are not the issue; density is.

prompt: An app recognises a scroll once the finger has moved 16 pixels. What happens on a 240 dpi screen compared with a 160 dpi one?

choices.text: It fires after a shorter movement of the finger
choices.why: Right. A tenth of an inch at 160 dpi becomes a fifteenth at 240.

choices.text: The scroll needs a longer movement on 240 dpi
choices.why: It is the other way round: a fifteenth of an inch instead of a tenth.

choices.text: The same: 16 pixels is 16 pixels
choices.why: The pixels are smaller on the denser screen, so the distance is shorter.

choices.text: The system refuses a size given in pixels
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; it just measures something different on each screen.

prompt: Match each platform to the unit its layouts are written in.

pairs.right: a plain number, read as the platform's own unit

prompt: A user turns up Android's display scaling because they see less well. One app grows with the setting and another stays small. What is the likeliest difference between them?

choices.text: The one that grows ships xxxhdpi images
choices.why: Image files decide sharpness, not whether a layout grows.

choices.text: The small one was built for an older Android version
choices.why: The version is not what decides it; the unit the layout was written in is.

choices.text: The one that grows wrote its layout sizes in sp
choices.why: sp follows the text size setting, not display scaling, and it is wrong for layout.

choices.text: The small one wrote sizes in pixels
choices.why: Right. Display scaling changes the density the app is given, and only sizes in dp follow it.

prompt: Using px = dp × (dpi / 160), how many pixels wide is a 48 dp button on a 320 dpi screen?
Put Android's density buckets in order, from lowest density to highest.
Which is right for the height of a row in the planner's session list?

choices.text: sp, so the row grows with the text
choices.why: Android's documentation says never to use sp for layout sizes; let the row grow with its content instead.

choices.text: dp, as for every layout size
choices.why: Right. sp is for text sizes only.

choices.text: px, because rows must line up exactly
choices.why: Pixels would make the row a different physical height on every screen.

choices.text: Any unit, since the system converts them all the same way
choices.why: They are converted differently: sp also follows the user's text size.

prompt: A phone's screen is 420 dpi. Which statement is true?

choices.text: The app crashes, because 420 is not a bucket
choices.why: Screens between buckets are ordinary; nothing fails.

choices.text: 48 dp is 126 px; images come from the nearest bucket
choices.why: Right. The sum works for any density; files come in fixed sizes.

choices.text: The system treats it as exactly 480 dpi for all sizes
choices.why: dp is converted with the screen's own density; buckets matter only for choosing files.

choices.text: dp cannot be used on it
choices.why: dp works on every screen; that is its purpose.

prompt: On Android, text sizes are written in ___, which follow the user's preferred text size, while layout sizes are written in dp.
Which scale factors do Apple's guidelines list for iPhone images?

choices.text: @1x only
choices.why: @1x is the baseline definition; iPhones are listed at higher scales.

choices.text: Whatever the app's developer chooses
choices.why: The scale is a property of the screen, set by Apple's hardware.

choices.text: @1x, @1.5x, @2x, @3x and @4x, like Android's buckets
choices.why: That ladder is Android's; iOS has far fewer steps.

choices.text: @2x and @3x
choices.why: Right. iPad is listed at @2x.

prompt: In React Native, a view has style width: 48. What is that 48?

choices.text: 48 dp on Android and 48 points on iOS
choices.why: Right. The plain number is the platform's own density-independent unit.

choices.text: 48 CSS pixels, as in a browser
choices.why: There is no browser here; the number is the platform's unit.

choices.text: 48 sp, so it scales with the text size
choices.why: Layout sizes do not follow the text size; only fontSize does.

choices.text: 48 physical pixels on every phone
choices.why: React Native's numbers are density-independent.

prompt: A one-pixel border is drawn on an @3x iPhone. How wide is it in points, and why does React Native round layouts to whole pixels?

choices.text: One point; rounding makes text sharper
choices.why: One pixel at @3x is a third of a point, and the rounding is about lines, as its documentation says.

choices.text: Three points; rounding saves memory
choices.why: Three pixels make one point at @3x, not the other way round.

choices.text: A third of a point; so a thin line neither vanishes nor doubles
choices.why: Right. Rounding errors on a one-pixel border make it disappear or grow to two.

choices.text: Half a point; rounding is needed only on Android
choices.why: Half a point is @2x; the documentation's example of the problem is iOS.

prompt: Match each way of sizing the title text to its platform.

pairs.right: React Native, scaled while allowFontScaling is true

right_distractors: CSS in a WebView, in pixels

prompt: According to the program's output, how many pixels across is the 24 dp icon at xxxhdpi?
The 48 dp button is 144 pixels across at xxhdpi and 48 at mdpi. How many times as many pixels does the whole square have at xxhdpi?

choices.text: 9 times
choices.why: Right. Three times as many in each direction is nine times as many in the square.

choices.text: 3 times
choices.why: 3 is the factor along one side; the square has two sides.

choices.text: 6 times
choices.why: That adds the two sides' factors instead of multiplying them.

choices.text: 144 times
choices.why: 144 is the side in pixels, not the ratio.

prompt: Why does the lesson not supply one 96x96 file for the icon and let every screen shrink it?

choices.text: Android refuses images larger than their bucket
choices.why: Nothing refuses it; the cost is quieter than that.

choices.text: A shrunk image cannot be tapped
choices.why: Touch has nothing to do with the image's pixels.

choices.text: An mdpi phone would decode sixteen times the pixels it shows
choices.why: Right. 96x96 against 24x24, for every icon, every time.

choices.text: iOS would show it at 96 points
choices.why: The displayed size comes from the layout's 24 points, not from the file.

prompt: Why can the lesson trust the numbers in density.ts's table without measuring a phone?

choices.text: They were copied from a real phone's settings screen
choices.why: No phone was used; the program computes them.

choices.text: They are arithmetic from the documented formula
choices.why: Right. Nothing in the table is measured.

choices.text: Node.js knows the density of the screen it runs on
choices.why: The program never asks the computer's screen anything.

choices.text: They are averages of many devices
choices.why: They are exact results of one sum, not averages.

prompt: Which of these should the planner keep as one vector file? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: The plus sign on the add-session button
choices.why: An icon is shapes, and shapes are described once.

choices.text: The check mark on a done session
choices.why: Another icon: one vector, sharp at every density.

choices.text: A photo a student attaches to a course
choices.why: A photo is pixels, and it stays a raster.

choices.text: The tab symbols
choices.why: Icons again, and on iOS SF Symbols are vectors already.

prompt: A designer hands over an SVG icon for the Android app. What does Android's documentation say happens to it?

choices.text: It goes into res/drawable-xxhdpi as it is
choices.why: Android does not read SVG itself, and a vector needs no density folder.

choices.text: It is shown in a WebView
choices.why: Nothing in the documentation suggests that.

choices.text: It is exported as five PNGs, one per bucket
choices.why: That throws away the reason to have a vector.

choices.text: It is converted to a vector drawable, one file in res/drawable
choices.why: Right. Vector Asset Studio does the conversion.

prompt: An app has a raster icon only in drawable-mdpi. On an xxhdpi phone, what does the user see?

choices.text: No icon, and an error in the log
choices.why: The system scales the best match; nothing fails.

choices.text: A sharp icon, because the system redraws it
choices.why: A raster cannot be redrawn, only stretched.

choices.text: An icon of the right size that looks soft
choices.why: Right. It is stretched three times, and a stretched raster goes soft.

choices.text: An icon a third of the size
choices.why: The size is kept; the system scales the file up to it.

prompt: A designer's mock-up shows the add-session button as 144 x 144 pixels, measured on an xxhdpi phone. What should the Compose code say?

choices.text: Modifier.size(48.dp)
choices.why: Right. 144 pixels at xxhdpi's 3x is 48 dp.

choices.text: Modifier.size(144.dp)
choices.why: That takes pixels for dp and makes the button three times too big.

choices.text: Modifier.size(144.sp)
choices.why: sp is for text, and 144 is still pixels.

choices.text: Modifier.size(72.dp)
choices.why: 72 is the hdpi pixel count of the button, not its size in dp.

prompt: Which of these would you write in sp?

choices.text: The gap between two session rows
choices.why: A gap is a layout size: dp.

choices.text: The 48 dp touch target
choices.why: A touch target is a layout size, and it is already dp.

choices.text: The size of the plus icon

choices.text: The size of a course's title

Two Android phones in the same bucket show a 48 dp button at very slightly different physical sizes. Why?

choices.text: One of them has a bug in its dp conversion
choices.why: The small difference is by design, as the lesson says.

choices.text: True densities differ a little from the bucket
choices.why: Right. dp removes the big factor between densities, not every millimetre.

choices.text: The user set a larger text size on one
choices.why: Text size changes sp, not a button sized in dp.

choices.text: dp is a promise in millimetres that phones break
